title: Week 3: EHR Foundations and Connected Clinical Systems
overview: This week examines electronic health records as longitudinal digital records that bring together clinical and administrative information. You will trace the development of EHRs from separate departmental systems toward connected care, distinguish clinical and administrative functions and primary and secondary uses, compare care settings, and follow information as it moves among EHRs and specialized clinical information systems.
objectives: Define an electronic health record and explain its purpose.
Describe the historical development and major functions of EHRs.
Distinguish clinical, administrative, primary, and secondary uses of EHR data.
Compare inpatient, ambulatory, long-term-care, and personal health records.
Explain how clinical information systems and decision support contribute to patient care.
Explain the main EHR functions and trace how information moves across connected healthcare systems.

concepts.definition: Supporting individual patient care and wider organizational activities through the entry, retrieval, review, updating, and sharing of authorized clinical and administrative information.

concepts.name: Interoperability

sections.title: 1. What an Electronic Health Record Is
sections.body:
An electronic health record, or EHR, is a digital record of health information used across time and healthcare services. It brings together the clinical and administrative information needed to support care. Authorized users can enter, retrieve, review, update, and share information according to their roles. The EHR supports both individual patient care and wider organizational activities.

An EHR may contain patient identification and demographic information; problems, diagnoses, allergies, medications, immunizations, and health history; clinical notes, care plans, orders, results, procedures, and discharge information; appointments, insurance information, authorizations, claims, and payments; and patient messages, educational materials, reminders, and information from connected systems.

The value of an EHR depends on accurate data, usable design, appropriate access, and reliable workflow.

sections.title: 2. How EHR Systems Developed
sections.body:
Healthcare organizations needed more timely access to patient information, safer and more standardized entry, and electronic checking. Laboratory, radiology, pharmacy, and other departments also required specialized digital systems. Organizations wanted information to support care, billing, reporting, quality improvement, and research.

During the 1980s, many systems focused on individual ancillary departments. During the 1990s, development moved toward broader electronic patient records, with a gradual shift from automating one department to connecting information across the organization. In the early 2000s, wider access and communication increased, EHR deployment expanded across healthcare settings, and the need to exchange information between systems made interoperability increasingly important.

Health information exchanges and personal health records extended access beyond one EHR. A selected U.S. policy milestone was the 2009 HITECH Act, which created incentives for eligible U.S. physicians and hospitals to adopt certified EHR technology. Specific laws and requirements differ between countries and healthcare systems.

sections.title: 3. EHR Functions and Uses
sections.body:
Clinical functions directly support assessment, diagnosis, treatment, monitoring, and communication about care. Examples include documentation, orders, results, medication management, prevention, chronic-care support, monitoring, and patient education.

Administrative functions support scheduling, authorization, claims, payment, inventory, and organizational operations. Clinical and administrative functions are connected: a clinical service can create documentation, supply-use, billing, and reporting data.

Primary use means using information directly to provide and coordinate care for a patient. Secondary use means using information for another legitimate purpose beyond the immediate encounter, such as quality improvement, population health, billing, research, education, or planning. Secondary use requires attention to data quality, privacy, access, and appropriate interpretation.

sections.title: 4. Care Settings and Patient Access
sections.body:
The core purpose of an EHR is similar across settings, but workflows and information needs differ. Inpatient EHRs support care during hospital admission and across hospital departments. Ambulatory EHRs support outpatient visits before, during, and after the encounter. Long-term-care EHRs support continuing care, minimum data requirements, and communication with hospitals.

Personal health records and patient portals give patients access to selected information and services. The setting, users, workflow, and information needs shape how each record is used.

sections.title: 5. Documentation, Orders, Results, and Medications
sections.body:
Clinical documentation records assessments, observations, diagnoses, interventions, and outcomes. It creates a shared account of what happened and why decisions were made. Complete and timely notes support communication, continuity of care, safety, billing, and legal requirements.

Templates and structured fields can improve consistency, but they may not capture every clinical detail. Free text can add context, but it may be harder to search and analyze.

In the orders-and-results workflow, an authorized clinician places an order, the order is transmitted to the responsible department, the service is completed, and the result returns to the EHR for review, interpretation, and follow-up. Clear links among the order, result, patient, time, and responsible professional support safety.

Medication orders can move electronically to pharmacy systems. The EHR may check allergies, duplicate therapy, dose, interactions, and other safety rules. Alerts support users but do not replace professional review and patient assessment.

sections.title: 6. Clinical Decision Support and Population Functions
sections.body:
Clinical decision support includes EHR-based checks, alerts, reminders, registries, templates, and related functions that support safety, prevention, chronic-care monitoring, and follow-up. EHRs can record immunizations, identify preventive services that are due, organize information about groups of patients, and support reminders and patient education.

Population-health tools summarize information across groups rather than one patient at a time. Immunization programs can use records to identify coverage and gaps. Appropriately governed EHR data may support research and clinical-trial activities. Interoperable connections can link hospitals with community, retail, and virtual-care providers, while remote monitoring can extend support to rural or high-risk populations.

sections.title: 7. Clinical Information Systems and the Shared Record
sections.body:
A clinical information system supports a particular area of patient care or clinical work. Examples include laboratory, radiology, pharmacy, cardiology, and procedure systems. These systems may create detailed information that becomes part of the wider EHR.

A laboratory information system supports orders, patient and test identification, specimen collection, tracking, testing, verification, reporting, and transmission of verified results to the EHR. Correct patient identification, units, reference ranges, and result status are essential.

A radiology information system supports imaging orders, scheduling, workflow, and reports. A picture archiving and communication system, or PACS, stores and displays medical images. A pharmacy information system receives medication orders and supports pharmacist review, preparation, medication information, dispensing, and exchange with the EHR and related systems.

The EHR acts as a central access point while specialized systems perform detailed departmental work. Interfaces and shared standards help systems exchange information. Breakdowns in identity, meaning, timing, or status can create clinical and administrative risk.

activities.title: Interpreting an Alert
activities.prompt: An EHR displays an alert about a possible medication interaction. What is the appropriate role of the alert?
options: It supports the user but does not replace professional review and patient assessment.
It automatically determines the final treatment decision.
It replaces the need to review the patient's record.
It removes the need for clinical judgment.
activities.debrief: Alerts can support users by checking interactions and other safety rules, but they do not replace professional review and patient assessment.

quiz.question: Which description best defines an electronic health record?
options: A digital record of health information used across time and healthcare services
A system used only for billing
A patient-access tool containing only educational materials
A departmental system used only for laboratory testing
quiz.rationale: An EHR is a digital record used across time and healthcare services that brings together clinical and administrative information needed to support care.

quiz.question: Which activity is a clinical function?
options: Monitoring patient results
Managing inventory
Submitting a claim
Scheduling equipment
quiz.rationale: Clinical functions directly support assessment, diagnosis, treatment, monitoring, and communication about care.

quiz.question: Which is an example of primary use of EHR data?
options: Reviewing a patient's history to provide care
Using information for organizational planning
Using information for research
Using information for quality improvement
quiz.rationale: Primary use means using information directly to provide and coordinate care for a patient.

quiz.question: Which is an example of secondary use of EHR data?
options: Population-health analysis
Entering a treatment order for the patient
Reviewing the patient's history during the encounter
Monitoring the patient's result for follow-up
quiz.rationale: Population health is a legitimate use beyond the immediate encounter and is therefore a secondary use.

quiz.question: Which record supports care during hospital admission and across hospital departments?
options: Inpatient EHR
Ambulatory EHR
Personal health record
Long-term-care EHR
quiz.rationale: An inpatient EHR supports care during hospital admission and across hospital departments.

quiz.question: What happens after an authorized clinician places an order in the orders-and-results workflow?
options: The order is transmitted to the department responsible for completing the service
The result is immediately discarded
The patient record is automatically closed
The order becomes a secondary-use report
quiz.rationale: After an authorized clinician places an order, it is transmitted to the responsible department for completion.

quiz.question: Which system stores and displays medical images?
options: Picture archiving and communication system
Laboratory information system
Pharmacy information system
Scheduling system
quiz.rationale: A picture archiving and communication system, or PACS, stores and displays medical images.

quiz.question: Which statement about clinical decision-support alerts is correct?
options: Alerts support users but do not replace professional review and patient assessment.
Alerts automatically determine the final treatment decision.
Alerts make review of the patient record unnecessary.
Alerts eliminate the need for clinical judgment.
quiz.rationale: Alerts can support safety checks, but professional review and patient assessment remain necessary.

quiz.question: What is the role of a clinical information system in the shared record?
options: It supports a particular area of patient care or clinical work and may contribute detailed information to the wider EHR.
It replaces the EHR as the only access point for all information.
It is used only for patient financial services.
It prevents information from moving between departments.
quiz.rationale: Clinical information systems support particular areas such as laboratory, radiology, or pharmacy and may create information that becomes part of the wider EHR.

quiz.question: Which information must remain consistent when systems exchange clinical information?
options: Patient identity, meaning, timing, and status
Only the patient's appointment preference
Only the department's inventory total
Only the patient education format
quiz.rationale: Breakdowns in identity, meaning, timing, or status can create clinical and administrative risk.
